Q: <glad/glad.h>: No such file or directory A:

The very simple reason is gcc or g++ doesn't recognize glad.h as a library file, because in order to do something like this

#include <mylib/lib.h>

you need to tell the compiler to search for include directories where mylib folder exists.
That basically means if you have

root/-|
      src/-|
           main.cpp
           glad.c
      include/-|
           glad/-
               glad.h

Then you must hit the command specifying the include directory

root\src> g++ -I/../include main.cpp main.c -o program -lGL -lGLU -lglut

That's it. gcc or g++ doesn't know what or where glad.h is because it simply doesn't know about the include directories

There is another way you can do it, without telling the compiler about include directories, that is explicitly including the header files

That is

#include "../include/glad/glad.h"

The difference is you need to use "" instead of <> and consider relative paths to the source you are working on.

The recommended approach is to use include directories specifier when using g++ or gcc directly or indirectly in the command line or powershell or terminal or whatever.

Q: Learning Claude A:

Hey even I’m just starting with this stuff too, so I feel you. Honestly, building something just for yourself is probably the fastest way to learn—tutorials only get you so far. I tried messing with “Claude Code Helper” the other day and, ugh, one of my tiny test scripts kept crashing. I didn’t even know why at first, so I just moved on and tried a simpler approach. Also showed it to a friend and they got confused by stuff I thought was obvious… kinda funny. Risks exist, obviously. Once I ran a snippet without double-checking, and thankfully nothing bad happened, but now I always keep experimental stuff in a separate folder. Little mistakes like that stick more than any guide. Making it public… haven’t done that yet. From what I’ve seen, getting it online is easy enough with Vercel or something, but making it usable for other people? That’s a whole different headache. Anyway… yeah. Just break a few things, fix them, figure it out as you go. That’s how it clicks, I think. Good luck!

Q: How to implement SQLAlchemy 2.0 transactions in FastAPI routes while maintaining test isolation with Savepoints? A:

Two things you'll probably eventually want for your fixture are scoped_sessions (mirroring production and improving interpretability) and to not have to worry about dirtying your database.

So, to answer your question, I shared my recommended solution here: https://stackoverflow.com/a/79911943/11039211

I recommend you make it so that commits can be used freely without actually commiting.

I recommend you don't patch every usage in every test, but instead use a single reference so one fixture can patch for all tests.

I recommend you add the following so you don't end up with corrupted savepoints despite your answers (and a few tests that check for a dirtied DB at the end of the suite):

# Source - https://stackoverflow.com/a/79911943
# Posted by Ivan Webber, modified by community. See post 'Timeline' for change history
# Retrieved 2026-03-21, License - CC BY-SA 4.0

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
addopts = "--strict-markers -W error::pytest.PytestCollectionWarning"
filterwarnings = [
    ...
    "error:nested transaction already deassociated from connection:sqlalchemy.exc.SAWarning",  # Savepoint corruption detector
    ...
]

Q: Multi-Sensor Data Fusion for Pile Strain Analysis A:

This is possible in Excel using the TREND or LINEST functions.
However, the presented data is not entirely consistent, so the function has to average them in some way. Is it supposed to be one smooth function (e.g. polynomial) covering all the data in the entire range, or separate functions for individual variants of the experiment?

Edit:
The OP did not specify exactly what the fit function should be. Assuming that it will be a single polynomial of 2nd degree fitted to all data in the entire range, you can get a line as shown. I did not take into account the weights of the points, because visually the change would be small, and the calculations would be complicated. But if necessary, weights can be included.
Formula used:
=TREND(R19:R37,P19:Q37,P19:P37^{1,2})
Columns g1 and g2 for point data contain x and x^2 respectively, and for data relating to the range <a, b> respectively: (a+b)/2 and (a^2+a*b+b^2)/3.
